4
For each band set \beta_{+}=\rho_{+}^{2}/(1+\rho_{+}) and choose the threshold
w(a)=\max\left\{\frac{M-\beta_{+}}{1-\beta_{+}},\,M-\frac{\beta_{+}}{2}(1-a^{2})\right\}.
If W_{1}\leq w(a), either Parseval or (5.7) with
\eta=1 gives \mathcal{W}_{\rho}\leq M throughout the band.
This single rule replaces individually chosen thresholds and Harris
parameters.
For W_{1}\geq w(a) and a\leq 2/5, concavity in squared
influences gives a single envelope for the whole region:
P_{f}(y)\geq(25w(0)/4)B_{y}(2/5).
Indeed, every squared coefficient is at most 4/25, and
B_{y}(\sqrt{s})\geq(25s/4)B_{y}(2/5) there. Sum and use
W_{1}\geq w(a)\geq w(0).
For 2/5\leq a\leq A_{*}, retain the exact cap C=\min(a,1-a)
on the other coefficients. Write (w(a)-a^{2})_{+}=kC^{2}+v, where
0\leq v<C^{2}. Packing gives
Q_{a}(y)=B_{y}(a)+kB_{y}(C)+B_{y}(\sqrt{v}).
Split only at a=1/2, the change of threshold formula, and
packing transitions w(a)-a^{2}=kC^{2}.
On each region, w(a)-a^{2} is affine in a^{2}.
The squared cap is affine in a^{2} below 1/2; above it,
(1-a)^{2} is convex as a function of a^{2}.
Lemma 4.10, applied to b(s)=B_{y}(\sqrt{s}),
shows that the packed profile is concave in a^{2}.
The reciprocal integral is therefore convex, as in
Lemma 4.9, so its maximum occurs at a
boundary value. These boundaries solve explicit linear or quadratic
equations in a and are reconstructed exactly. The initial envelope
also covers the boundary a=2/5.
The resulting 20 clocks pass (5.9), using
36 integration intervals and 91 supporting-line evaluations.
For a\geq A_{*}, each right endpoint verifies M_{\rho}(A_{*})>0
for the local deficit in (3.2);
Lemma 3.5 and Theorem 3.4 cover
the band. Lemma 5.3 reduces the scalar gates to
eight correlation endpoint checks and supplies the prior credit
analytically. The replay checks those gates, the four local signs,
and exact adjacency of the source and correlation intervals.
Lemma 5.4 now covers every source.
∎
5.5. The two-coordinate band
In the last intermediate band, convexity still handles a\leq 2/3
with one retained coordinate. Above that cutoff we use both largest
singleton coefficients, through either a profile comparison or the
exact two-coordinate entropy bound.
Theorem 5.7.
Theorem 1.2 holds on 39/40\leq\rho\leq 49/50.
Computer-assisted proof.
Set A_{*}=76043/100000 and M=150614067/200000000.
Use the preceding threshold and the same cap rule on
0\leq a\leq 2/3. Four clock comparisons suffice, using nine
integration intervals and 21 supporting-line evaluations.
The one-coordinate local sign M_{\rho}(A_{*})>0 covers a\geq A_{*}.
It remains to cover 2/3<a<A_{*}. Restrict the certified rational
partition of [0,A_{*}]\times[0,1/2] to this region.
Before each split, a rectangle [a_{0},A]\times[b_{0},B] is contracted
as follows: first replace a_{0} by \max(a_{0},b_{0}), then A
by \min(A,1-b_{0}), and finally B by \min(B,A,1-a_{0}).
Every feasible point with a\geq b and a+b\leq 1 survives this
operation. Each binary split retains both closed children.
We first cover 3a+7b\geq 64/25 by a uniform moment bound. Apply Lemma 3.8 to the noisy conditional
mean from Proposition 3.7, with
\lambda=1-\rho^{2}<1/20. Its centered third moment is
6\rho^{4}abc. Since |c|\leq b\leq 1-a and a\geq 2/3,
its absolute value is at most 6a(1-a)^{2}\leq 4/9.
Thus the compensation error is less than 1/5000.
The second and fourth centered moments increase with |c|, so we
may replace it by b in their negative terms.
For these moment bounds define h:\{-1,1\}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} by
h(x,y)=\rho ax+\rho by+\rho^{2}bxy, with uniform expectation.
Lemma 3.9
and 9/13<\log 2<7/10 give
(5.10)
\frac{\Phi(\rho)-A_{\rho}(f)}{1-\rho^{2}}\geq\frac{17}{12}[\rho^{2}(a+b)-1]-\frac{\rho^{2}b}{5}+\frac{9}{13}-\frac{\mathbb{E}h^{2}}{2}-\frac{\mathbb{E}h^{4}}{5}-\frac{1}{198}.
Here 1/[5000(1-\rho^{2})]\leq 1/198.
For fixed \rho, the right side is concave in (a,b).
Its minimum on 2/3\leq a\leq A_{*}, a+b\leq 1, and 3a+7b\geq 64/25 therefore occurs at one of the four vertices
(2/3,2/25), (2/3,1/3), (A_{*},1-A_{*}), and (A_{*},(64/25-3A_{*})/7).
For fixed a,b, both moments are polynomials in \rho^{2} with
nonnegative coefficients, so the right side is also concave in
\rho^{2}. Evaluation at the two correlation endpoints gives eight
rational values, all greater than 1/1000.
This proves the local claim without a mean partition.
Exactly 22 certified leaves meet a>2/3. Seventeen satisfy
3\max(a_{0},2/3)+7b_{0}\geq 64/25 and are covered by the moment bound.
The remaining five use Lemma 5.4, with the
two-coordinate threshold (5.7) and a one- or
two-coordinate profile. Their clocks use 11 integration intervals
and 40 supporting-line evaluations. Lemma 5.3
reduces the scalar conditions to two correlation endpoint checks,
and the one-coordinate local sign propagates from the right endpoint.
The replay reconstructs the full source tree, verifies the
classification of every retained leaf, and checks all thresholds,
envelopes, and integrals. The script two_core_moment_verify.py
checks the elementary constants and the eight rational values in
(5.10). A separate exact audit expands
the moments and checks the polynomial on the whole squared-correlation
interval using Bernstein coefficients. The one-coordinate argument
covers the omitted region, including a=2/3.
Compression completes the assertion for arbitrary sources.
∎
6. Entropy interpolation and spectral transfer
By (2.6), \rho G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)=D(T_{\rho}f)-\rho\atanh\rho.
Thus, at
a hypothetical positive gap, it is enough to rule out
D(T_{\rho}f)\leq\rho u, where u=\atanh\rho. We do this by
transforming g=T_{\rho}f to h=\arcsin g. The choice reflects
entropy curvature: (\arcsin)^{\prime}(t)=\sqrt{\Phi^{\prime\prime}(t)}, so
Cauchy–Schwarz gives
(\arcsin b-\arcsin a)^{2}\leq(b-a)(\atanh b-\atanh a) for a<b.
On each cube edge,
entropy production exceeds the Dirichlet energy of h by a
nonnegative remainder. Globally, h is close in L_{2} to
(\pi/2)g, so spectral completion exposes the Fourier energy of the
noisy source. The profile budget converts the remaining coordinate
sum into a scalar inequality.
Throughout this section 0<\rho<1 and
f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} is nonconstant.
Write u=\atanh\rho, g=T_{\rho}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to(-1,1), and
h=\arcsin g:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to(-\pi/2,\pi/2).
Define the scalar entropy correction and its average by
(6.1)
\Psi(t)=t^{2}\log 2-\Phi(t)=H(t)-(1-t^{2})\log 2,\qquad\mathcal{J}=\mathbb{E}\Psi(g).
Thus \mathcal{J} measures
the excess of conditional entropy above its elementary quadratic
lower bound. It is nonnegative by the entropy series and vanishes
at the scalar values 0,\pm 1. The next lemma uses this same excess
to control the error in replacing \arcsin g by (\pi/2)g.
All expectations use the uniform probability measure. By (1.3),
G_{f}(\rho)>0 implies
\mathbb{E}H(g)<H(\rho)-\Phi(\mu)\leq H(\rho).
6.1. A sharp scalar error estimate
The arcsine transform is close to \frac{\pi}{2}g at a cost measured by the
entropy remainder \mathcal{J}. This bound lets the later spectral
argument work directly with the Fourier coefficients of f.
Lemma 6.1.
For every -1\leq t\leq 1,
(6.2)
(\arcsin t-\frac{\pi}{2}t)^{2}\leq C_{*}\Psi(t),\qquad C_{*}:=\frac{(\frac{\pi}{2}-1)^{2}}{{\log 2}-1/2}.
In particular,
\|h-\frac{\pi}{2}g\|_{2}^{2}\leq C_{*}\mathcal{J}.
Proof.
By (2.7), \Psi\geq 0 on [-1,1].
We compare the two sides by their even power series. Put
a_{n}=4^{-n}\binom{2n}{n} and write
U(t)=C_{*}\Psi(t)-(\arcsin t-\tfrac{\pi}{2}t)^{2}=\sum_{k\geq 1}b_{k}t^{2k}.
The choice of C_{*} makes b_{1}=0. The standard series for
\arcsin t and its square give, for n\geq 1,
(6.3)
b_{n+1}=\frac{c_{n}-C_{*}}{2(n+1)(2n+1)},\qquad c_{n}=2\pi(n+1)a_{n}-\frac{2}{a_{n}}.
Thus c_{n} is the threshold determining the sign of the coefficient.
These thresholds decrease with n. Indeed, the Wallis integrals give
\frac{\pi}{2}a_{n}=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n}x\,dx<\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n-1}x\,dx=\frac{1}{2na_{n}},
so \pi na_{n}^{2}<1. Using
a_{n+1}/a_{n}=(2n+1)/(2n+2), we obtain
c_{n+1}-c_{n}=\frac{\pi n(2n+1)a_{n}^{2}-2(n+1)}{(n+1)(2n+1)a_{n}}<0.
It remains to locate the single sign change. We have
c_{3}=\frac{5\pi}{2}-\frac{32}{5}<C_{*}<\frac{9\pi}{4}-\frac{16}{3}=c_{2}.
For the logarithm bounds, retain the first two terms in
\log 2=2\sum_{j\geq 0}((2j+1)3^{2j+1})^{-1} and bound the
remaining denominators below by 5.
Consequently b_{2},b_{3}>0 and b_{k}<0 for every k\geq 4.
The series converge absolutely at t=1, where U(1)=0.
This endpoint identity and the single sign change determine the
sign on the whole interval: for x=t^{2}\in[0,1], each negative
term satisfies b_{k}x^{k}\geq b_{k}x^{3} when k\geq 4. Hence
U(t)\geq b_{2}x^{2}+\left(b_{3}+\sum_{k\geq 4}b_{k}\right)x^{3}=b_{2}x^{2}(1-x)\geq 0.
Evenness proves the scalar inequality on [-1,1].
The ratio of its left-hand side to \Psi(t) tends to C_{*} as
t\to 0, proving optimality. Averaging proves the function inequality.
∎
6.2. An exact edge refinement
We now bound the excess of entropy production over arcsine energy.
The main result below combines these edge remainders over any chosen
set of coordinates and gives a common budget for their profile heights.
For v>0, define
(6.4)
\zeta(v)=\arcsin(\tanh v)=\arctan(\sinh v),\qquad R(v)=v-\frac{\zeta(v)^{2}}{\tanh v},
with R(0)=0. On a centered edge with endpoint magnitude \tanh v,
the production is v\tanh v and the arcsine energy is \zeta(v)^{2}.
Thus R(v) is the excess production per unit of edge size.
To evaluate this excess at the dictator entropy, use F from
(4.1) and put
(6.5)
\ell_{u}(a)=F^{-1}(F(u)/a)\quad(a>0),\qquad\ell_{u}(0)=0.
Indeed, H(\rho)/(\rho a)=F(u)/a, so \ell_{u}(a) is precisely
the profile parameter associated with entropy H(\rho) and
coordinate size \rho a. We call it a profile height. The next
proposition bounds the sum of the corresponding coordinate costs
by the total entropy production, which is the common budget used
in the spectral argument.
Proposition 6.2 (Simultaneous arcsine refinement).
Let f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} be nonconstant,
0<\rho<1, g=T_{\rho}f, and h=\arcsin g.
For every A\subseteq[n],
{D(g)}\geq\operatorname{Dir}(h)+\rho\sum_{i\in A\colon|\widehat{f}(i)|>0}|\widehat{f}(i)|R\left(F^{-1}\left(\frac{E_{\rho}(f)}{\rho|\widehat{f}(i)|}\right)\right).
Put u=\atanh\rho and \ell_{i}=\ell_{u}(|\widehat{f}(i)|),
using (6.5). If G_{f}(\rho)>0, then
{D(g)}\geq\operatorname{Dir}(h)+\rho\sum_{i\in A}|\widehat{f}(i)|R(\ell_{i}).
If G_{f}(\rho)>0, the common profile budget satisfies
\sum_{i}|\widehat{f}(i)|\ell_{i}\leq D(g)/\rho.
We prove this by comparing each edge with a centered edge and then
averaging. The following convexity allows the edge entropies to be
replaced by their common mean.
Lemma 6.3.
The function R is strictly increasing and strictly convex on
(0,\infty). Define
(6.6)
\mathcal{R}(e,d)=dR(F^{-1}(e/d))\qquad(e,d>0).
This function is jointly convex, increasing in d, and decreasing in e.
It extends continuously to d=0 with value zero, and
(e,q)\mapsto\mathcal{R}(e,|q|) is jointly convex.
Proof.
Direct differentiation gives
R^{\prime}(v)=[1-\arctan(\sinh v)/\sinh v]^{2}.
For s>0, \arctan s/s strictly decreases from 1 to 0,
because \arctan s>s/(1+s^{2}). Thus R^{\prime},R^{\prime\prime}>0.
By Lemma 4.1, the inverse of F is convex and
decreasing. Composition with the increasing convex function R
shows that R\circ F^{-1} is convex and decreasing.
The perspective argument in the proof of Lemma 4.2
therefore gives joint convexity of \mathcal{R}; its decrease in e
follows directly from the defining formula.
Increasing d increases both nonnegative factors in \mathcal{R}.
Also F^{-1}(e/d)\to 0 as d\downarrow 0, which proves the
continuous extension. Monotonicity in d and the triangle inequality
give convexity of the even extension.
∎
Lemma 6.4.
Let x=c+d, y=c-d belong to (-1,1), with d>0, and put
b=\frac{\atanh x-\atanh y}{2},\qquad A=\frac{\arcsin x-\arcsin y}{2},\qquad e=\frac{H(x)+H(y)}{2}.
Then
db-A^{2}\geq dR(F^{-1}(e/d)).
Equality holds when c=0, and the inequality is strict when
c\neq 0. A zero-length edge contributes zero to both sides, with
the extension in Lemma 6.3.
Proof.
Put a=(\atanh x+\atanh y)/2 and \ell=F^{-1}(e/d).
Lemma 4.4 gives b\geq\ell.
The identities x=\tanh(a+b) and y=\tanh(a-b) imply
d=\frac{\sinh b\cosh b}{\cosh^{2}a+\sinh^{2}b},\qquad A=\arctan\!\left(\frac{\sinh b}{\cosh a}\right).
For t>0, the function q(t)=(1+t^{2})(\arctan t/t)^{2}
is strictly increasing: its logarithmic derivative is
2[(\arctan t)^{-1}-t^{-1}]/(1+t^{2})>0. Hence
\frac{A^{2}}{d}=\tanh b\,q\!\left(\frac{\sinh b}{\cosh a}\right)\leq\tanh b\,q(\sinh b)=\frac{\zeta(b)^{2}}{\tanh b}.
Hence db-A^{2}\geq dR(b)\geq dR(\ell) by
Lemma 6.3.
The first inequality is strict unless a=0, equivalently c=0;
in that case e/d=F(b) and both inequalities are equalities.
∎
Proof of Proposition 6.2.
Write e=E_{\rho}(f). On coordinate fibers let e_{i} be the average
endpoint entropy and q_{i}=(g_{+}-g_{-})/2 the signed half-difference.
Then \mathbb{E}e_{i}=e and \mathbb{E}q_{i}=\rho\widehat{f}(i).
Average the inequality in Lemma 6.4 and apply Jensen’s inequality
to the convex even extension of \mathcal{R} from (6.6). For |\widehat{f}(i)|>0 this gives
\mathcal{D}_{i}(g)-\operatorname{Dir}_{i}(h)\geq\rho|\widehat{f}(i)|R\left(F^{-1}\left(\frac{e}{\rho|\widehat{f}(i)|}\right)\right)\quad(|\widehat{f}(i)|>0).
The other coordinates have nonnegative remainders by edge
Cauchy–Schwarz, including those with |\widehat{f}(i)|=0. Summing proves the first inequality.
Positive gap gives e<H(\rho); monotonicity in e therefore gives the positive-gap bound.
Finally, Proposition 4.3 gives
D(g)\geq\sum_{i}B_{e}(\rho|\widehat{f}(i)|). Positive gap and monotonicity in e
bound this sum below by \sum_{i}B_{H(\rho)}(\rho|\widehat{f}(i)|)=\rho\sum_{i}|\widehat{f}(i)|\ell_{i}, proving the profile budget.
∎
6.3. Spectral completion
Completing a square transfers transformed energy to the noisy
source. It also yields entropy inequalities for the finite reversible
Markov semigroups defined in Section 2.5.
We retain their general form because the argument uses the reversible
edge identity and the spectrum of the generator. We then return to
the cube and the projection argument.
Theorem 6.5 (Entropy bounds under reversible noise).
Let P_{s}=e^{-s\mathcal{L}} be a Markov semigroup on a finite
probability space (\Omega,\nu), reversible with stationary measure \nu.
Expectations use \nu, and
\operatorname{Dir}(h)=\mathbb{E}[h\mathcal{L}h] for h:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}.
For every f:\Omega\to[-1,1] and s>0,
\begin{split}\mathbb{E}H(P_{s}f)&\geq(\log 2)(1-\mathbb{E}f^{2})+\frac{9}{2s^{3/2}}\int_{0}^{s}t^{3/2}\operatorname{Dir}(P_{t}f)\,dt,\\
\mathbb{E}\sqrt{1-(P_{s}f)^{2}}&\geq 1-\mathbb{E}f^{2}+\frac{5}{2\sqrt{s}}\int_{0}^{s}\sqrt{t}\,\operatorname{Dir}(P_{t}f)\,dt.\end{split}
Lemma 6.6 (Spectral transfer).
Let A be self-adjoint on a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
If \gamma>0 and A+\gamma I is positive definite, then
\langle v,Av\rangle+\gamma\|v-w\|^{2}\geq\langle w,\gamma A(\gamma I+A)^{-1}w\rangle
for all v,w.
Proof.
In an orthonormal eigenbasis of A, use the scalar identity
\lambda x^{2}+\gamma(x-y)^{2}=(\lambda+\gamma)\left(x-\frac{\gamma y}{\lambda+\gamma}\right)^{2}+\frac{\gamma\lambda}{\gamma+\lambda}y^{2},
and discard the square. Negative eigenvalues are allowed as long
as \lambda>-\gamma.
∎
Theorem 6.7 (Entropy and smoothed energy).
Let P_{s}=e^{-s\mathcal{L}} be a Markov semigroup on a finite
probability space (\Omega,\nu), reversible with stationary measure \nu.
Write \operatorname{Dir}(h)=\mathbb{E}[h\mathcal{L}h] for h:\Omega\to\mathbb{R},
and D(h)=\mathbb{E}[(\mathcal{L}h)\atanh h] for h:\Omega\to(-1,1).
For every f:\Omega\to[-1,1] and s>0,
\frac{9}{2}\operatorname{Dir}(P_{s}f)\leq D(P_{s}f)+\frac{3}{2s}\left[\mathbb{E}H(P_{s}f)-(\log 2)(1-\mathbb{E}f^{2})\right].
Endpoint values are understood by approximation.
Proof.
Set g=P_{s}f. Edgewise Cauchy–Schwarz gives
\operatorname{Dir}(\arcsin g)\leq D(g) for every reversible
Markov generator. Lemma 6.1 gives
\|\arcsin g-\frac{\pi}{2}g\|_{2}^{2}\leq(12/7)\mathbb{E}\Psi(g).
Use Lemma 6.6 with \gamma=7/(8s).
This choice makes the interpolation penalty
\gamma(12/7)\mathbb{E}\Psi(g)=3\mathbb{E}\Psi(g)/(2s) exactly match the
entropy coefficient in the conclusion. The identity
\mathbb{E}H(g)-(\log 2)(1-\mathbb{E}f^{2})=\mathbb{E}\Psi(g)+(\log 2)(\|f\|_{2}^{2}-\|g\|_{2}^{2})
then separates the transform error from the squared norm lost under
noise. If f_{\lambda} is the projection onto the eigenspace of
\mathcal{L} with eigenvalue \lambda\geq 0, square completion gives
D(g)+\frac{3}{2s}\bigl[\mathbb{E}H(g)-(\log 2)(1-\mathbb{E}f^{2})\bigr]\geq\sum_{\lambda}\left[\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\frac{\gamma\lambda}{\gamma+\lambda}e^{-2s\lambda}+\frac{3\log 2}{2s}(1-e^{-2s\lambda})\right]\|f_{\lambda}\|_{2}^{2}.
For a positive eigenvalue, put x=2s\lambda and factor out
\lambda e^{-2s\lambda}. The remaining scalar multiplier is
\frac{7\pi^{2}/4}{7+4x}+3(\log 2)\frac{e^{x}-1}{x}\geq\frac{9}{2}\qquad\text{for }x\geq 0.
Indeed, use \pi^{2}/4>123/50, \log 2>9/13, and
(e^{x}-1)/x\geq 1+x/2+x^{2}/6.
After multiplication by 7+4x, the difference from 9/2 is
at least 3(300x^{3}+1425x^{2}-525x+56)/650>0;
the quadratic part has negative discriminant -43575.
Summing the scalar bound gives the claimed estimate.
The zero eigenspace contributes zero. Apply the argument first to
(1-\varepsilon)f, then let \varepsilon\downarrow 0.
∎
Lemma 6.8 (Hellinger interpolation).
Let J(t)=\sqrt{1-t^{2}} and
\Theta(t)=\int_{0}^{t}(1-x^{2})^{-3/4}\,dx.
For -1\leq t\leq 1,
|\Theta(t)-\Theta(1)t|^{2}\leq 2[\Theta(1)-1]^{2}[J(t)-J(t)^{2}]\leq 6[J(t)-J(t)^{2}].
Proof.
The substitution x=1-y^{4} gives
\Theta(1)=4\int_{0}^{1}(2-y^{4})^{-3/4}\,dy.
Using 2^{3/4}<17/10 and the tangent bound
(1-y^{4}/2)^{-3/4}\geq 1+3y^{4}/8 gives
\Theta(1)>43/17>5/2.
The chord bound for the convex function (2-x)^{-3/4},
together with 2^{3/4}>5/3, gives \Theta(1)<68/25<3.
In particular, 2[\Theta(1)-1]^{2}<3698/625<6.
By symmetry take 0\leq t\leq 1, and put
\varphi(t)=\sqrt{J(t)-J(t)^{2}}.
Direct differentiation gives
-\varphi^{\prime\prime}(t)=3\sqrt{1-J(t)}/[4J(t)^{7/2}] and
\Theta^{\prime\prime}(t)=3t/[2J(t)^{7/2}]. Hence
\Theta^{\prime\prime}(t)/[-\varphi^{\prime\prime}(t)]=2\sqrt{1+J(t)} decreases strictly
from 2\sqrt{2} to 2.
It follows that the second derivative of
w(t)=\sqrt{2}[\Theta(1)-1]\varphi(t)-\Theta(1)t+\Theta(t)
changes sign once, from positive to negative.
Since w(0)=w^{\prime}(0)=w(1)=0, its derivative first increases and
then decreases; thus w increases and then decreases, and w\geq 0.
Convexity gives \Theta(t)\leq\Theta(1)t, proving the bound.
Finally, the ratio |\Theta(t)-\Theta(1)t|^{2}/[J(t)-J(t)^{2}] tends to
2[\Theta(1)-1]^{2} as t\to 0, proving optimality.
∎
Proposition 6.9.
In the setting of Theorem 6.7, let
D_{J}(h)=\mathbb{E}[(\mathcal{L}h)h/J(h)].
Then
\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{Dir}(P_{s}f)\leq D_{J}(P_{s}f)+\frac{1}{2s}\left[\mathbb{E}J(P_{s}f)-1+\mathbb{E}f^{2}\right].
Proof.
Put g=P_{s}f. Edgewise Cauchy–Schwarz gives
\operatorname{Dir}(\Theta(g))\leq D_{J}(g).
Use the same cancellation as in Theorem 6.7,
now with \gamma=1/(12s) and interpolation constant 6.
Their product is 1/(2s), the coefficient of the Hellinger
remainder in the conclusion.
For x\geq 0, the scalar multiplier is greater than
(25/4)/(1+6x)+(e^{x}-1)/x\geq 5/2.
To verify the last inequality, use
(e^{x}-1)/x\geq 1+x/2+x^{2}/6 and multiply by 12(1+6x).
The resulting polynomial is 12x^{3}+38x^{2}-102x+57.
Since x^{3}\geq 3x-2, it is at least
38x^{2}-66x+33>0, whose discriminant is -660.
The spectral summation from Theorem 6.7
proves the proposition.
∎
For Boolean sources on the cube, P_{s}=T_{e^{-s}} and the endpoint
correction vanishes. Thus
\frac{9}{2}\operatorname{Dir}(T_{\rho}f)\leq D(T_{\rho}f)+3\mathbb{E}H(T_{\rho}f)/[-\log(\rho^{2})].
More generally, differentiating \mathbb{E}H(P_{s}f) gives D(P_{s}f).
Proof of Theorem 6.5.
Multiply the inequality in Theorem 6.7 by s^{3/2} and
integrate from zero. Since \frac{d}{ds}\mathbb{E}H(P_{s}f)=D(P_{s}f),
the first inequality follows by an integrating factor.
For the second, use \frac{d}{ds}\mathbb{E}J(P_{s}f)=D_{J}(P_{s}f) and
multiply the inequality in Proposition 6.9 by \sqrt{s}.
The boundary terms at zero vanish because both entropies are bounded.
∎
6.4. From variance to entropy production
The next lemma removes the unknown variance \Var(g) and entropy
error \mathcal{J} from a spectral bound. At positive gap, it
replaces their combination by an explicit baseline and a nonnegative
correction for the source mean. Here \mathcal{J} is the entropy
correction defined in (6.1).
Lemma 6.10 (Transfer of a spectral baseline).
Let f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}, 0<\rho<1, and g=T_{\rho}f.
For \Lambda,\Gamma>0, define
(6.7)
\eta_{\Lambda,\Gamma}(\rho)=\Gamma\bigl[\tfrac{1}{2}-(1-{\rho^{2}})\log 2\bigr]-\Lambda{\rho^{2}}.
If G_{f}(\rho)>0 and \eta_{\Lambda,\Gamma}(\rho)\geq 0, then
\Lambda{\Var(g)}-\Gamma\mathcal{J}\geq\Lambda{\rho^{2}}-\Gamma\Psi(\rho)+\eta_{\Lambda,\Gamma}(\rho)\mu^{2}.
Proof.
Parseval gives \Var(g)\leq\rho^{2}(1-\mu^{2}), and positive gap gives
0\leq\mathcal{J}<\Var(g)\log 2+\Psi(\mu)-\Phi(\rho).
The latter inequality uses \mathbb{E}g^{2}={\Var(g)}+\mu^{2} and the actual
information inequality \mathbb{E}\Phi(g)>\Phi(\rho)+\Phi(\mu).
The assumption \eta_{\Lambda,\Gamma}(\rho)\geq 0 implies
\Lambda-\Gamma{\log 2}\leq\Gamma(1/2-{\log 2})/{\rho^{2}}<0.
Since \Psi(\mu)\leq({\log 2}-1/2)\mu^{2},
\displaystyle\Lambda{\Var(g)}-\Gamma\mathcal{J}
\displaystyle\geq(\Lambda-\Gamma{\log 2}){\Var(g)}+\Gamma\Phi(\rho)-\Gamma\Psi(\mu)
\displaystyle\geq(\Lambda-\Gamma{\log 2}){\rho^{2}}(1-\mu^{2})+\Gamma\Phi(\rho)-\Gamma({\log 2}-1/2)\mu^{2}
\displaystyle=\Lambda{\rho^{2}}-\Gamma\Psi(\rho)+\eta_{\Lambda,\Gamma}(\rho)\mu^{2}.\qed
Only \Var(g) is centered; \mathcal{J} remains the actual
interpolation error. The explicit compact parameters below satisfy the
transfer condition throughout their range by an analytic estimate.
7. Coordinate projections and the spectral bound
We prove the uniform spectral criterion that handles every source
below the local cutoff. Retain the coordinates above a threshold and
charge the discarded coordinates to the same profile budget. We first bound the variance of the retained
source and the energy of the discarded arcsine field. Combining these
bounds gives the scalar criterion in Theorem 7.6.
Throughout this section, write \rho=\tanh u, g=T_{\rho}f,
and h=\arcsin g. We retain the entropy correction \mathcal{J}
from (6.1) and the profile height \ell_{u}
from (6.5). For K\subseteq[n], define
(7.1)
P_{K}h=\mathbb{E}[h\mid X_{K}].
This averages over the coordinates outside K and is the orthogonal
projection onto functions of X_{K}. In Fourier language it keeps
exactly the terms with S\subseteq K; the remainder h-P_{K}h
contains every term using an outside coordinate. This decomposition
allows separate estimates for dependence carried by the retained
coordinates and for the energy needed to support the remainder.
Throughout this section,
f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} is nonconstant and increasing.
We retain the full budget D(g)/\rho from
Proposition 6.2. This gives a direct lower bound for entropy
production at every positive gap.
7.1. An influence bound for bounded functions
Conditional sources take values in [-1,1]. The following theorem
bounds their variance by an explicit cost for each influence, without
assuming monotonicity.
We express the variance bound in terms of the function
(7.2)
\psi(a)=\min\left\{\frac{a+a^{2}}{2},\frac{2a(1-a/4)}{\log(4/a)}\right\}\quad(0<a\leq 1),\qquad\psi(0)=0.
Theorem 7.1 (Variance and influences).
For every g:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1] and every K\subseteq[n],
\Var(P_{K}g)\leq\sum_{i\in K}\psi(\|\partial_{i}g\|_{1}).
In particular, \Var(g)\leq\sum_{i}\psi(\|\partial_{i}g\|_{1}).
The estimate is a quantitative form of the following influence inequality.
Theorem 7.2 (Talagrand’s influence inequality
[25, 7]).
There is a universal constant C>0 such that, for every
f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R},
\Var(f)\leq C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\|\partial_{i}f\|_{2}^{2}}{1+\log(\|\partial_{i}f\|_{2}/\|\partial_{i}f\|_{1})}.
We now prove the explicit bounded-function estimate used here.
Proof of Theorem 7.1.
Fourier expansion gives
\Var(g)=\sum_{i}\int_{0}^{1}\|T_{\sqrt{s}}\partial_{i}g\|_{2}^{2}\,ds.
Indeed, a mode of degree j contributes s^{j-1} in each of its
j coordinates. Fix i and write a=\|\partial_{i}g\|_{1}.
Since |\partial_{i}g|\leq 1, the integrand is at most
(1-s)a^{2}+sa by its Fourier expansion, and at most
a^{2/(1+s)} by hypercontractivity.
Integrating the first bound gives (a+a^{2})/2.
For the second, substitute r=(1-s)/(1+s) and use
\log(1+r)\geq r\log 2 on [0,1]:
\int_{0}^{1}a^{2/(1+s)}\,ds=2a\int_{0}^{1}\frac{a^{r}}{(1+r)^{2}}\,dr\leq 2a\int_{0}^{1}(a/4)^{r}\,dr=\frac{2a(1-a/4)}{\log(4/a)}.
Both bounds apply to each coordinate’s integral separately, so
we may take their minimum before summing. Zero influences contribute
zero. For a projection, apply the bound to P_{K}g: conditional
expectation contracts each derivative in L^{1}, and \psi is increasing.
∎
For monotone g, \partial_{i}g\geq 0, so
\|\partial_{i}g\|_{1}=\widehat{g}(i). This is the form used for the Boolean source below.
7.2. Retaining the pivot energy in a martingale decomposition
We next bound the energy of the part discarded by projection,
using the martingale entropy argument of Falik and Samorodnitsky
[9, Theorem 2.2 and Lemma 2.3].
Reveal the coordinates one at a time and subtract successive
conditional expectations. These differences are the Doob martingale
increments: each records the additional dependence revealed at that
step. Its Fourier terms all contain the newly revealed coordinate,
so it already contributes one unit of degree before the other
coordinates are counted. Keeping that contribution strengthens the
log-Sobolev estimate used below.
Lemma 7.3 (Martingale energy).
Let h:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} and K\subseteq[n].
Set
V=\|h-P_{K}h\|_{2}^{2}\enskip\text{and }b_{K}=\sum_{i\notin K}(\mathbb{E}|\partial_{i}h|)^{2}.
For every real \lambda, we have
\operatorname{Dir}(h-P_{K}h)\geq\left(1+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)V-\frac{e^{\lambda-1}}{2}b_{K}.
When V and b_{K} are positive, the stronger nonlinear form is
\operatorname{Dir}(h-P_{K}h)\geq V+\frac{V}{2}\log\frac{V}{b_{K}}.
Proof.
Order the coordinates of K before its complement, and let
h_{i}:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} be the Doob increments of h in this
order, so
h_{i}=\mathbb{E}[h\mid X_{1},\ldots,X_{i}]-\mathbb{E}[h\mid X_{1},\ldots,X_{i-1}].
Each has the form h_{i}=X_{i}g_{i}(X_{<i}), with
g_{i}:\{-1,1\}^{i-1}\to\mathbb{R}. Thus
\Ent(h_{i}^{2})=\Ent(g_{i}^{2}) and
\operatorname{Dir}(h_{i})=\|h_{i}\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{Dir}(g_{i}).
The log-Sobolev part of Theorem 3.1, applied
to g_{i}, gives
\Ent(h_{i}^{2})\leq 2[\operatorname{Dir}(h_{i})-\|h_{i}\|_{2}^{2}].
Also h_{i}=\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{i}h\mid X_{1},\ldots,X_{i}], so
\mathbb{E}|h_{i}|\leq\mathbb{E}|\partial_{i}h|.
For a real random variable Z with v=\mathbb{E}Z^{2}>0, use the
probability measure dQ=Z^{2}\,dP/v. Jensen gives
\mathbb{E}_{Q}\log|Z|\geq-\log\mathbb{E}_{Q}|Z|^{-1}=\log(v/\mathbb{E}|Z|), hence
\Ent(Z^{2})\geq v\log[v/(\mathbb{E}|Z|)^{2}].
Zeros of Z have zero Q-measure, so approximation justifies this
calculation.
Applying this bound and the log-sum inequality to the increments
whose pivot is outside K yields
\sum_{i\notin K}\Ent(h_{i}^{2})\geq V\log(V/b_{K}).
Their Fourier supports are disjoint: a nonconstant mode belongs
to the increment at its last revealed coordinate. Hence their squared
norms sum to V and their energies sum to
\operatorname{Dir}(h-P_{K}h).
This proves the second inequality. The inequality
V\log(V/b_{K})\geq\lambda V-e^{\lambda-1}b_{K} gives the first inequality. If b_{K}=0, every outside derivative
vanishes, so V=0; when V=0 the latter inequality is immediate.
∎
7.3. A signed Fourier operator and the source projection
We combine the discarded-field estimate with the retained-source
variance bound. The resulting inequality assigns one cost to each
retained coordinate; the discarded singletons are paid for by the
unused part of the common profile budget.
There are two choices in the comparison. The parameter t is the
energy level assigned to discarded modes of degree at least two;
\gamma is the penalty for replacing the arcsine transform by a
multiple of the noisy source. It must also offset any negative
singleton multiplier. Accordingly, for t\geq 2, choose
(7.3)
\gamma>\max\{0,\tfrac{1}{2}e^{2t-3}-t\},\qquad k(s)=\frac{\gamma s}{\gamma+s}.
For a selected coordinate set K, Lemma 7.3,
applied to h with \lambda=2t-2, gives
\operatorname{Dir}(h)\geq\operatorname{Dir}(P_{K}h)+t\|h-P_{K}h\|_{2}^{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}e^{2t-3}\sum_{i\notin K}\widehat{h}(i)^{2}.
Here monotonicity of h implies
\mathbb{E}|\partial_{i}h|=\widehat{h}(i)\geq 0.
The quadratic form on the right defines a self-adjoint operator
A\chi_{S}=\lambda_{S}\chi_{S}. Its Fourier eigenvalues are
(7.4)
\lambda_{S}=\begin{cases}0,&S=\varnothing,\\
|S|,&\varnothing\neq S\subseteq K,\\
t-\tfrac{1}{2}e^{2t-3},&S=\{i\},\ i\notin K,\\
t,&|S|\geq 2,\ S\not\subseteq K.\end{cases}
The multiplier records how much energy the preceding estimate
assigns to each Fourier mode. A mode entirely inside K retains
its actual degree, while an outside mode of degree at least two is
assigned the common lower bound t. Outside singletons incur a
correction and may have a negative multiplier. The choice of
\gamma ensures that adding \gamma I makes the operator positive,
so the square-completion lemma applies with the transferred
multiplier k from (7.3).
Lemma 7.4.
With R and C_{*} from (6.4) and
(6.2), if G_{f}(\rho)>0,
{D(g)}\geq\rho\sum_{i\in K}\widehat{f}(i)R(\ell_{i})-\gamma C_{*}\mathcal{J}+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\sum_{S}k(\lambda_{S})\rho^{2|S|}\widehat{f}(S)^{2}.
Proof.
The simultaneous remainder bound in Proposition 6.2
first gives
{D(g)}\geq\rho\sum_{i\in K}\widehat{f}(i)R(\ell_{i})+\operatorname{Dir}(h).
Every multiplier
in (7.4) is greater than -\gamma, even
when an outside singleton multiplier is negative. Apply
Lemma 6.6 to this operator, with
v=h and w=\frac{\pi}{2}g,
then use \|h-\frac{\pi}{2}g\|_{2}^{2}\leq C_{*}\mathcal{J} from
Lemma 6.1.
This proves the lemma. The constant mode of
h need not vanish. It is included in the error norm,
whereas its quadratic-form multiplier is zero. Here k(0)=0 even when \widehat{g}(\varnothing)=\mu\neq 0.
∎
Theorem 7.1, applied to f and K, gives \Var(P_{K}f)\leq\sum_{i\in K}\psi(\widehat{f}(i)).
Choose 0<z<u and retain the coordinates above the threshold
(7.5)
\beta=\frac{F(u)}{F(z)},\qquad K=\{i:\ell_{i}\geq z\}=\{i:\widehat{f}(i)\geq\beta\}.
Define the nonnegative coefficients
(7.6)
\begin{split}\Delta_{2}&=[k(t)-k(2)]\rho^{4},\\
\Delta_{1}&=[k(t)-k(1)]{\rho^{2}},\\
\Delta_{o}&=[k(t)-k(t-\tfrac{1}{2}e^{2t-3})]{\rho^{2}},\qquad\tau=\Delta_{o}\frac{\beta}{z}.\end{split}
The inequalities t\geq 2 and monotonicity of k imply
\Delta_{1}\geq\Delta_{2}\geq 0.
Proposition 7.5.
If G_{f}(\rho)>0,
\begin{split}{D(g)}\geq{}&\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}k(t){\Var(g)}-\gamma C_{*}\mathcal{J}-\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\tau\frac{D(g)}{\rho}\\
&+\sum_{i\in K}\widehat{f}(i)\left[\rho R(\ell_{i})+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\tau\ell_{i}-\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\Delta_{2}\frac{\psi(\widehat{f}(i))}{\widehat{f}(i)}-\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}(\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2})\widehat{f}(i)\right].\end{split}
Proof.
Relative to the constant multiplier k(t) on nonconstant modes,
the raw Fourier accounting is
\displaystyle{D(g)}\geq{}
\displaystyle\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}k(t){\Var(g)}-\gamma C_{*}\mathcal{J}+\rho\sum_{i\in K}\widehat{f}(i)R(\ell_{i})
\displaystyle-\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\left[\Delta_{2}\Var(P_{K}f)+(\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2})\sum_{i\in K}\widehat{f}(i)^{2}+\Delta_{o}\sum_{i\notin K}\widehat{f}(i)^{2}\right].
Indeed, the singleton coefficient inside K is \Delta_{1}. For
every degree j\geq 2,
[k(t)-k(j)]\rho^{2j}\leq\Delta_{2}: a nonpositive coefficient may be dropped,
and otherwise k(j)\geq k(2) and \rho^{2j}\leq\rho^{4}. Thus the cost is
at most
\Delta_{2}\Var(P_{K}f)+(\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2})\sum_{i\in K}\widehat{f}(i)^{2}\leq\sum_{i\in K}\bigl[\Delta_{2}\psi(\widehat{f}(i))+(\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2})\widehat{f}(i)^{2}\bigr].
The remaining cost is exactly
\Delta_{o}\sum_{i\notin K}\widehat{f}(i)^{2}.
To bound this cost, Lemma 4.1 shows that
\ell_{u}(a)/a is decreasing: at v=\ell_{u}(a) it equals
vF(v)/F(u), while v increases with a.
Consequently \widehat{f}(i)^{2}\leq(\beta/z)\widehat{f}(i)\ell_{i} outside K.
The profile budget in Proposition 6.2 gives
\sum_{i\notin K}\widehat{f}(i)\ell_{i}\leq D(g)/\rho-\sum_{i\in K}\widehat{f}(i)\ell_{i}.
Insert these two bounds into the inequality in Lemma 7.4 and collect
terms. This proves the proposition.
∎
7.4. One bound for all retained coordinates
We now compare the spectral baseline with the cost of each unit of
the profile budget. This treats every retained coordinate uniformly,
so the largest influence enters only as an upper bound on the range
of a scalar function.
The preceding bound has one spectral baseline and one correction
for each retained coordinate. Dividing that coordinate’s correction
by its profile contribution a\ell_{u}(a) gives the scalar cost
below. Bounding every such cost by the same number lets us sum
over an arbitrary number of coordinates using the common production
budget. Using \psi from (7.2) and the corrections
in (7.6), define, for 0<a\leq 1,
(7.7)
\mathcal{Q}_{u}(a)=\frac{\rho[\ell_{u}(a)-R(\ell_{u}(a))]+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\Delta_{2}\psi(a)/a+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}(\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2})a}{\ell_{u}(a)}.
Theorem 7.6 (Uniform spectral bound).
Let f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} be nonconstant and increasing,
\rho=\tanh u with u>0, and \alpha=\max_{i}|\widehat{f}(i)|.
Choose 0<z<u, t\geq 2, and \gamma satisfying
(7.3). With \beta,\tau,\mathcal{Q}_{u} as in
(7.5)–(7.7), put
b=\max\left\{\rho+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\tau,\sup_{\beta\leq a\leq\alpha}\mathcal{Q}_{u}(a)\right\}.
If G_{f}(\rho)>0 and the mean-transfer coefficient from
(6.7) satisfies
\eta_{\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}k(t),\gamma C_{*}}(\rho)\geq 0, then
\frac{D(T_{\rho}f)}{\rho}\geq\frac{\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}k(t)\rho^{2}-\gamma C_{*}\Psi(\rho)}{b}.
At such a positive gap, G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)>0 whenever
\frac{\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}k(t)\rho^{2}-\gamma C_{*}\Psi(\rho)}{u}>\max\left\{\rho+\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\tau,\sup_{\beta\leq a\leq\alpha}\mathcal{Q}_{u}(a)\right\}.
Proof.
Apply Lemma 6.10 to
Proposition 7.5. Its retained contribution is
\sum_{i\in K}\widehat{f}(i)\ell_{i}[\rho+\pi^{2}\tau/4-\mathcal{Q}_{u}(\widehat{f}(i))].
Because \rho+\pi^{2}\tau/4-b\leq 0, the profile budget in Proposition 6.2 bounds this below by
(\rho+\pi^{2}\tau/4-b)D(g)/\rho.
Consequently
D(g)\geq\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}k(t)\rho^{2}-\gamma C_{*}\Psi(\rho)+(\rho-b)\frac{D(g)}{\rho}.
Rearrange and use G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)=D(g)/\rho-u.
∎
A condition proved for all a\leq\alpha also covers every smaller
maximum influence. This simple monotonicity eliminates the partition
in the source parameter. Lemma 3.6 covers
\alpha\geq 1-2e^{-u} throughout the compact range. The spectral
calculation therefore uses this moving cutoff throughout as well.
No separate uniform dictator-neighborhood theorem is needed for
the qualitative argument.
7.5. An analytic bound for the spectral cost
Supporting lines to the convex remainder R give convex upper bounds
for the spectral cost on every positive height interval. This reduces
the remaining calculation to endpoint values. The key is a global
shape property of the entropy profile.
Lemma 7.7 (Convex upper bounds for the scalar costs).
Fix u,c>0 and \Delta_{1}\geq\Delta_{2}\geq 0, and put \rho=\tanh u.
In the cost (7.7), replace \psi(a) by either
(a+a^{2})/2 or 2a(1-a/4)/\log(4/a).
Set a=F(u)/F(v) and replace [v-R(v)]/v by
1-R^{\prime}(c)+\frac{cR^{\prime}(c)-R(c)}{v}.
The resulting function is a convex upper bound for
\mathcal{Q}_{u}(F(u)/F(v)) on 0<v\leq u.
The latter replacement increases the expression by at most
\rho(v-c)^{2}/(4v).
With the same choice for \psi, replacing
\rho[v-R(v)]/v instead by \pi^{2}/(4v) also gives
a convex upper bound.
Proof.
Put a=F(u)/F(v). Since F is decreasing, 0<v\leq u implies
0<a\leq 1 and \ell_{u}(a)=v. Either formula in
(7.2) is at least \psi(a); its coefficient
in (7.7) is nonnegative.
Convexity of R gives R(v)\geq R(c)+R^{\prime}(c)(v-c) and
cR^{\prime}(c)-R(c)\geq 0, since R(0)=0. The tangent replacement is
therefore an upper bound consisting of a constant and a nonnegative
multiple of 1/v.
For the quadratic choice, the remaining terms are
\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\left[\frac{\Delta_{2}}{2v}+\left(\Delta_{1}-\frac{\Delta_{2}}{2}\right)\frac{F(u)}{vF(v)}\right].
For the logarithmic choice, use
2(1-a/4)/\log(4/a)=2\int_{0}^{1}(a/4)^{r}\,dr to obtain
\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\left[2\Delta_{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(F(u)/4)^{r}}{vF(v)^{r}}\,dr+(\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2})\frac{F(u)}{vF(v)}\right].
Both are nonnegative combinations of the convex functions
1/[vF(v)^{r}], 0\leq r\leq 1, from Lemma 4.1.
Integration preserves their convexity, proving the first assertion.
For the error estimate, put p=\arctan(\sinh v)/\sinh v.
The bounds x/(1+x^{2})\leq\arctan x\leq x give
\operatorname{sech}^{2}v\leq p\leq 1. Differentiating R^{\prime}=(1-p)^{2} yields
0\leq R^{\prime\prime}(v)=2\coth v(1-p)(p-\operatorname{sech}^{2}v)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\tanh^{3}v\leq\tfrac{1}{2},
because the two nonnegative factors have sum \tanh^{2}v.
Taylor’s theorem now gives
0\leq R(v)-R(c)-R^{\prime}(c)(v-c)\leq(v-c)^{2}/4.
Multiplication by \rho/v proves the stated increase from the
tangent replacement; it does not include the earlier choice for \psi.
Finally, convexity of \arcsin on [0,1] gives
\arcsin x\leq(\pi/2)x. By (6.4),
\rho[v-R(v)]=\rho\frac{\arcsin^{2}(\tanh v)}{\tanh v}\leq\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\rho\tanh v\leq\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}.
Replacing the first term by \pi^{2}/(4v) thus leaves a sum of
convex functions, proving the alternative bound.
∎
A fixed choice of the formula for \psi and of c therefore requires
only two endpoint checks
on any closed height interval. Choosing c=\sqrt{v_{-}v_{+}} on
[v_{-},v_{+}] bounds the tangent error uniformly by
\rho(\sqrt{v_{+}}-\sqrt{v_{-}})^{2}/4.
This follows by maximizing (v-c)^{2}/v at the endpoints.
More generally, intervals equally spaced in \sqrt{v} make this
error decay quadratically in their number.
7.6. An explicit choice on the compact noise range
The inverse profile determines the upper end of the retained height
range. Bounds on the growth of e^{2v}F(v) give an explicit upper
height and control its influence. The compact calculation therefore
needs no inverse roots or curvature estimates.
Lemma 7.8 (Inverse bound).
Let u>2 and e^{2-u}\leq a\leq 1. For
v=u+(2u+1)\log a/(4u+1),
F^{-1}(F(u)/a)\leq v\leq u,\qquad\frac{F(u)}{F(v)}\leq e^{-2(u-v)}\frac{2u+1}{2v+1}.
Proof.
Define the scaled profile
(7.8)
S(s)=e^{2s}F(s).
Lemma A.1 gives
1/(2s+1)<S^{\prime}(s)/S(s)<2/(2s+1) for s\geq 2.
The case a=1 is exact. Otherwise put w=F^{-1}(F(u)/a)<u.
Since -F^{\prime}/F>1,
-\log a=\int_{w}^{u}(-F^{\prime}/F)\,ds>u-w,
so w>u+\log a\geq 2. On [w,u] we also have
-F^{\prime}/F=2-S^{\prime}/S<2-1/(2u+1). Integrating gives
-\log a<(2-1/(2u+1))(u-w), hence w<v\leq u.
Finally, integration on [v,u] gives
\log[S(u)/S(v)]\leq\log[(2u+1)/(2v+1)].
Using (7.8) proves the second bound.
∎
Throughout 45951/20000\leq u\leq 8, use the single choice
z=\log u+\frac{u}{25}-\frac{2}{5},\qquad t=\frac{49u}{100}+\frac{7}{5},\qquad\gamma=\frac{1}{2}e^{49u/50-1/5}+e^{9u/20+1/4}.
Thus \gamma>e^{2t-3}/2 identically. Also 0<z<2u/3 and
t>2, using \log 2>1/2 and \log u\leq u/2 for u\geq 2.
The transfer condition is analytic as well. The ratio \gamma/t increases because
\gamma^{\prime}/\gamma\geq 9/20>t^{\prime}/t, and the exponential series gives
\gamma(9/4)>85/12>(5/2)t(9/4). Since
1-\rho^{2}<1/20, C_{*}>8/5, \pi^{2}/4<5/2, and
\log 2<7/10, the normalized transfer margin exceeds
(8/5)(1/2-7/200)-5/7=26/875.
Set c(u)=1-2e^{-u} throughout this interval. This cutoff satisfies u+\log c(u)>2:
u>9/4, and e^{2}>22/3, e^{1/4}>41/32 give
c(u)>e^{-1/4}. Let
v_{+}(u)=u+(2u+1)\log c(u)/(4u+1).
By Lemma 7.8, this explicit height covers
all a\leq c(u), and v_{+}(u)>u-1/4>2u/3.
On [z,2u/3], use the logarithmic formula for \psi in
Lemma 7.7, with the tangent to R at z.
On [2u/3,v_{+}(u)], use the quadratic formula with the tangent
at v_{+}(u). Each bound is convex in height, so its two endpoints
suffice. At the upper endpoint, substitute the upper bound for
F(u)/F(v_{+}(u)) from Lemma 7.8; both
influence costs increase with this argument.
The certificate checks these four height endpoints and the
discarded-coordinate inequality on 24 closed noise intervals.
All parameters are explicit functions of u; there are no fitted
parameter families or stored height records. Fourth-order Taylor
bounds retain cancellation on each noise interval. The separate
audit checks the original costs throughout the extended height
range. Appendix A records the replay scope.
8. Completion of the qualitative proof
The same uniform spectral bound can reach the local entropy region
even as that region shrinks toward a dictator. We first state the
local threshold, then choose spectral parameters whose losses remain
small enough to meet it. Together these estimates complete the proof of CK.
8.1. A local junction valid for both error masses
The local entropy comparison covers sufficiently small dictator
distance at each correlation. The following explicit boundary will
also be the starting point of the spectral comparison.
Recall the distance \delta(f) to a signed dictator from
(2.1). To describe the local region, put
(8.1)
u_{\delta}=\log\frac{3}{2\delta}\quad(\delta>0),\qquad d_{-}(u)=\frac{3}{2}e^{-u}.
Thus u\leq u_{\delta} is equivalent to \delta\leq d_{-}(u).
Lemma 8.1.
Let f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} satisfy 0<\delta(f)\leq 1/64.
Then CK holds for 0\leq\rho\leq\tanh u_{\delta(f)},
at arbitrary output mean.
Proof.
Put \delta=\delta(f). By Lemma 3.5,
it suffices to prove the local comparison at \rho=\tanh u_{\delta}.
Let p=4\delta^{2}/(9+4\delta^{2}) and
\rho_{\delta}=1-2p=\tanh u_{\delta}.
Elementary entropy bounds give
H(\rho_{\delta}(1-2\delta))\geq H_{\rm b}(\delta),
H_{\rm b}(\delta)/\delta\geq\log(1/\delta)+1-\delta, and
H_{\rm b}(p)/p\leq 2\log(1/\delta)+\log(9/4)+4\delta^{2}/9+1.
Using the local deficit (3.2) and dividing
M_{\rho_{\delta}}(1-2\delta) by 2\delta p,
its positivity follows from
2(1-4\delta^{2}/9)(\log(1/\delta)+1-\delta)>(1+8\delta/9)(2\log(1/\delta)+\log(9/4)+4\delta^{2}/9+1).
The difference is at least
1-\log(9/4)-\delta[2+(8/9)(2\log(1/\delta)+\log(9/4)+1)]-(4\delta^{2}/9)(2\log(1/\delta)+3).
Use \log 64<25/6 and \log(9/4)<13/16.
The functions \delta\log(1/\delta) and \delta^{2}\log(1/\delta) increase in this
range, so substitution at \delta=1/64 bounds the difference
below by 65/4608>1/80.
Theorem 3.4 now gives the claim.
∎
8.2. A spectral comparison reaching the local neighborhood
For the qualitative argument, choose the square-completion parameter
on the scale e^{u}, with spectral level t on the scale u/2.
Its entropy penalty is then of order ue^{-u}, the same order as
the spectral gain at the local distance threshold. Two simple savings
make these estimates overlap: we keep the arcsine correction and
combine the degree corrections before estimating their remaining loss.
The stronger uniform margins used for stability are established in
the companion paper [29].
Proposition 8.2.
Let f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} be increasing, and let
\rho=\tanh u with u\geq 8. If
\delta(f)\geq(3/2)e^{-u}, then
G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)>0 whenever G_{f}(\rho)>0.
Proof.
Apply Theorem 7.6 with
z=7/2,t=u/2+1, and \gamma=e^{u}/4.
Write h=e^{-u}, a_{0}=1-3h, and
N=(\pi^{2}/4)k(t)\rho^{2}-\gamma C_{*}\Psi(\rho) for the
spectral baseline. The distance assumption gives \alpha\leq a_{0}.
We will compare the baseline with the discarded-coordinate cost
and every retained-coordinate cost on \beta\leq a\leq a_{0}.
First, the arcsine contribution has a useful saving. The function
\arcsin^{2}x/x increases on (0,1), so for 0<v\leq u we have
\rho[v-R(v)]\leq\arcsin^{2}\rho=\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}-2\arctan h\,\bigl(\pi-2\arctan h\bigr)<\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}-4h.
Here h<1/2500, since e>27/10, and
h/(1+h^{2})\leq\arctan h\leq h proves the last inequality.
Replacing the arcsine numerator by this positive constant gives a
convex upper cost for either formula for \psi, as in
Lemma 7.7. Use the logarithmic formula through
a=1/8 and the quadratic formula thereafter. Only the heights
7/2, \ell_{u}(1/8), and \ell_{u}(a_{0}) need to be checked.
We use 12/5<\pi^{2}/4<5/2 and 1<C_{*}<12/7.
The parameter condition follows from e>2, and the transfer
condition follows from \gamma>10t and 1-\rho^{2}<4h^{2}.
The bounds
k(t)\rho^{2}>t-\frac{1}{10},\qquad\gamma C_{*}\Psi(\rho)<\frac{1}{300}
give N/u>6/5+2/u. Indeed,
t^{2}/\gamma=(u+2)^{2}e^{-u} and 4te^{-2u} decrease from u=8,
and \Psi(\rho)\leq H(\rho)\leq(2u+1)e^{-2u}.
For discarded coordinates,
k(t)-k(t-e^{2t-3}/2)=\frac{\gamma^{2}e^{2t-3}/2}{(\gamma+t)(\gamma+t-e^{2t-3}/2)}<\frac{e^{u}}{2(e-2)}.
Together with (4.2), this gives
\beta\leq\frac{1001}{1000}\frac{2u+1}{8}e^{7-2u},\qquad\tau<\frac{1001}{1000}\frac{(2u+1)e^{7-u}}{56(e-2)}.
The upper bound for u\tau decreases for u\geq 8.
Using e>27/10 at u=8 therefore gives
N-u(\rho+\pi^{2}\tau/4)>1/3 throughout this range.
For the first retained height, the profile bound gives
\beta<1/200 and \log(4/\beta)\geq(3u-5)/2.
For the latter inequality, compare
2u-7+\log(32000/[1001(2u+1)]) with (3u-5)/2:
the difference is positive at 8 and has positive derivative.
Since \Delta_{2}<t-1 and \Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}<2, the cost at
v=7/2 is less than
\frac{5}{7}\left(1+\frac{2u}{3u-5}+\frac{1}{100}\right)<\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{u}.
At a=1/8, the profile derivative first gives
\ell_{u}(1/8)>u-\log 8>4, then \ell_{u}(1/8)>u-6/5. The quadratic cost is less than
\frac{5}{2}\frac{5/4+9u/32}{u-6/5}<\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{u}.
For both comparisons, clearing positive denominators gives a
quadratic that is positive and increasing for u\geq 8.
The logarithmic cost is smaller at this junction, since
\log 2>31/45. These costs are therefore below N/u.
It remains to compare the top height v=\ell_{u}(a_{0}) with the
baseline. The profile derivative gives u-v\leq 7h/4.
In the quadratic cost, combine the degree corrections before
estimating them: its numerator is at most
\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\left[1+\Delta_{1}a_{0}+\frac{\Delta_{2}}{2}(1-a_{0})\right]-4h.
This keeps the degree-one loss 1-k(1). Put d=1-a_{0}=3h.
Using 1-k(1)<1/\gamma and k(1)-k(2)/2<1/\gamma, we obtain
1-k(1)\rho^{2}a_{0}-k(2)\rho^{4}d/2\leq(1+d)(\gamma^{-1}+4h^{2})=4h(1+4h+3h^{2}).
Also u-v\leq 7h/4 and u\geq 8 imply
1-\frac{u}{v}(a_{0}+\rho^{2}d/2)\geq\frac{5}{4}h,\qquad\frac{4u}{v}(1+4h+3h^{2})<\frac{101}{25}.
Writing \overline{\mathcal{Q}}_{u}(a_{0}) for the upper cost and
using u/v\geq 1 in the arcsine saving now gives
\displaystyle\frac{N-u\overline{\mathcal{Q}}_{u}(a_{0})}{h}
\displaystyle>3\left(\frac{u}{2}+\frac{9}{10}\right)-\frac{101}{10}-\frac{3}{7}(2u+1)+4
\displaystyle=\frac{9u}{14}-\frac{134}{35}\geq\frac{46}{35}>0.
The four terms record the spectral gain, degree-correction cost,
entropy penalty, and arcsine saving, respectively; their sum is a
positive linear function of u. All costs are therefore below N/u,
proving the derivative assertion by
Theorem 7.6.
∎
8.3. Completion of the proof
The compact spectral calculation uses the same moving local cutoff
throughout. It consequently gives a derivative criterion for every
possible positive-gap source without a separate neighborhood theorem.
Proposition 8.3.
For every increasing f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}, if
49/50\leq\rho\leq\tanh 8 and G_{f}(\rho)>0, then
G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)>0.
Computer-assisted proof.
Lemma 3.6 rules out positive gap when
\alpha\geq 1-2e^{-u}. For the remaining sources,
Theorem 7.6 gives D(T_{\rho}f)>\rho u, hence
G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)>0. The certificate verifies this criterion on
24 closed noise intervals covering [45951/20000,8], always
with the cutoff 1-2e^{-u}.
Since \log 9<45951/20000<\atanh(49/50), both the local cutoff
and the spectral cover apply throughout the stated range.
Appendix A gives the verification details.
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.2.
Proposition 3.15 gives 0\leq\rho\leq 457/500;
Theorems 5.6 and 5.7 give
457/500\leq\rho\leq 49/50. Fix an increasing nonconstant source.
We claim that every positive-gap point with 49/50\leq\rho<1
has G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)>0. Proposition 8.3 proves
this through u=8. For u\geq 8, Lemma 8.1
excludes positive gap when \delta(f)\leq(3/2)e^{-u}; the dictator
case is exact. Proposition 8.2 covers every
remaining source. The claim follows.
Since G_{f}(1)=-\Phi(\mu)\leq 0, the differential barrier in
Lemma 2.2 now proves CK throughout [49/50,1].
Compress an arbitrary source at the fixed correlation in question;
constants have zero information. All intervals are closed, and the
endpoint assertions are 0\leq 0 and H(\mu)\leq\log 2.
∎

Appendix A Certificates and reproducibility
Fixed low-correlation signs are checked by rational series bounds;
the other transcendental signs are checked on complete closed rational
domains by outward-rounded Arb arithmetic [15]. The moving-cap source
boundaries are quadratic algebraic numbers reconstructed exactly. A strict sign is accepted only when
the entire enclosure has that sign; a nonfinite enclosure or one
containing zero is inconclusive. Exact rational and algebraic arithmetic checks coverage.
Every supporting line is valid by convexity; its explicit integral
is accepted only after the required denominator and final signs pass.
The compact inverse profile is bounded analytically. Bisections retain both children unless infeasibility is
proved. Data-free scripts check the finite constants in the analytic
argument of Proposition 8.2 and the local
junction in Lemma 8.1.
A.1. The compact certificate
The qualitative file qualitative_compact_certificate.json
covers [45951/20000,8] by 24 closed rational noise intervals:
eight equal intervals through 4, followed by 16 intervals of
length 1/4. The cutoff is 1-2e^{-u} throughout, and
Lemma 3.6 covers every larger influence.
The single explicit parameter rule uses 96 height endpoint inequalities
from Lemma 7.7. No height records or fitted
parameter families are stored. The split is 2u/3, and
Lemma 7.8 supplies the upper endpoint without
root calculations. Exact adjacency checks verify the noise partition.
The replay qualitative_compact_verify.py recomputes every
scalar sign at 256 bits. It clears positive denominators and expands
logarithms of profile ratios before interval evaluation, retaining
cancellation without changing the signs. The transfer condition is
proved analytically. The separate qualitative_compact_audit.py
uses independently derived unscaled formulas, 384-bit arithmetic,
and first-order bounds on the full extended height domain.
Both verify the full stated domain and its moving influence cutoff. Neither uses an optimizer or inverse roots.
A.2. Files and replay scope
The certificate data and verification code are available in the
GitHub repository linked below. The low-correlation argument
uses ten fixed endpoint inequalities and no correlation partition.
The middle-range checks use ten scalar endpoint gates, five local
endpoint signs, and 29 clocks with 56 integration intervals and 152
supporting-line evaluations. The two-coordinate mean bound uses eight
fixed rational signs and no mean partition. The unbounded endpoint
argument is analytic; its checker verifies the finite constants used
in that argument, without sampling the unbounded domain.
From the bundle root, install requirements.txt and run
python3 verify.py. This checks the file manifest and runs
the ten numerical stages supporting the exact theorem. Each stage
recomputes its signs and domain coverage and writes its report to a
fresh output directory. Optimized Python is rejected because the
verifiers use assertions. The separate stability paper has its own
package and stronger quantitative checks; none of them is an input
to this exact proof. The README.md records the build and replay
commands. Only current inputs are included. The certificate data and verification code are available at
https://github.com/vukhacky/courtade-kumar-conjecture/.
A.3. Growth of the scaled profile
This estimate gives the explicit inverse bound in
Lemma 7.8 using only first derivatives.
Lemma A.1.
For the scaled profile S in (7.8) and v\geq 2,
1<(2v+1)S^{\prime}(v)/S(v)<2.
Proof.
Put q=e^{-2v}. The entropy formula gives
S(v)=2v+1+\sum_{n\geq 1}(2v+1+c_{n})q^{n},\qquad c_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k(k+1)}\in(0,1/2].
Termwise differentiation gives
2-(4v+3)q/(1-q)^{2}\leq S^{\prime}(v)<2.
The subtracted term decreases for v\geq 2; e^{4}>54 bounds
it by 594/2809<1/4, so S^{\prime}>7/4.
Equation (4.2) gives
2v+1<S(v)\leq(2v+1)(1+q)/(1-q).
Since (1+q)/(1-q)<55/53<7/4, the asserted ratios follow.
∎
A.4. The central energy remainder
The next estimate completes the affine interpolation argument in
Proposition 3.15. Its proof reduces the entire
noise interval to a concave polynomial and one endpoint value.
Lemma A.2.
For 0\leq\rho\leq 457/500,
\frac{76-49\rho^{2}}{57}H(\rho)<(1-\rho)\left(1+\rho-\frac{193027}{250000}\rho^{2}\right).
Proof.
Let V(\rho) be the right side minus the left side. We show that
V decreases and check its value at the right endpoint.
The entropy series gives
\frac{V^{\prime}(\rho)}{\rho}=-2\left(1+\frac{193027}{250000}\right)+\frac{4}{3}+\frac{98}{57}\log 2+\frac{579081}{250000}\rho+\sum_{n\geq 1}d_{n}\rho^{2n},
where d_{n}=4/[3(2n+1)]-49(n+1)/[57n(2n-1)].
We have
d_{1}<-80/63, d_{2}<-17/105, d_{3}<-4/105, and d_{4}<0.
For n\geq 5, the bound d_{n}<1/64 follows from
84n^{3}-1280n^{2}+5227n+1152=(84n+64)(n-8)^{2}+875n-2944>0.
Indeed, this polynomial is
1344n(4n^{2}-1) times the difference between 1/64 and the
upper bound obtained by replacing 49/57 by 6/7.
Also \rho^{10}/[64(1-\rho^{2})]<1/25 on the stated interval.
Therefore \log 2<7/10 gives V^{\prime}(\rho)/\rho<P(\rho), where
P(\rho)=-\frac{362581}{375000}+\frac{579081}{250000}\rho-\frac{80}{63}\rho^{2}-\frac{17}{105}\rho^{4}-\frac{4}{105}\rho^{6}.
Now P^{\prime\prime}<-5/2, P(3/4)<-19/10000, and
0<P^{\prime}(3/4)<17/200. Completing the square in its quadratic
tangent bound gives
P(\rho)\leq P(3/4)+P^{\prime}(3/4)^{2}/5<-1/2500.
Thus V decreases. Finally V(457/500)>1/50000 by the
rational logarithm bounds below, proving the claim.
∎
For completeness, all ten low-correlation comparisons use explicit
finite series. Reduce a positive rational logarithm argument to
x\in[1,2] by extracting powers of 2. With z=(x-1)/(x+1),
the first twelve terms of
2\sum_{j\geq 0}z^{2j+1}/(2j+1) underestimate \log x by at
most 2z^{25}/[25(1-z^{2})]. The same formula bounds \log 2.
For the Fourier constants, twelve terms of the alternating
arctangent series in
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239) give rational bounds for
\pi; squaring rational endpoints bounds each square root.
The file low_correlation_verify.py performs these rational
operations with no input certificate. The separate
low_correlation_audit.py checks the same constants directly
with Arb at 384 bits.
A.5. A rational curvature bound
The following calculation supplies the curvature estimate used in
Lemma 5.3. It involves only polynomial
coefficients and rational inequalities.
Lemma A.3.
For 0\leq x\leq 43/500 and 3/4\leq M\leq 83/100, put
C=3-2M+(-3+5M)x+(1-4M)x^{2}+Mx^{3} and
V=(1/2+3x-3x^{2}+x^{3})/C.
Then -7+30x<V^{\prime\prime}<0 and V^{\prime}<2.
Proof.
All derivatives in this proof are with respect to x.
The denominator is positive: C\geq 67/50, since
C(0)=3-2M\geq 67/50 and
C^{\prime}\geq 3/4-(116/25)(43/500)>0.
Expanding the numerator of -V^{\prime\prime} and bounding its coefficients over the
given interval for M gives
-C^{3}V^{\prime\prime}\geq 15-60x-54x^{3}-7x^{5}>8.
In particular, V^{\prime\prime}<0.
Also V^{\prime}(0)=(21/2-17M/2)/(3-2M)^{2}<2, so V^{\prime}<2.
For the lower bound, write
C^{3}(V^{\prime\prime}+7-30x)=\sum_{j=0}^{3}P_{j}(x)(83/100-M)^{j}.
Direct expansion, discarding positive terms and using x<1/10,
gives the following bounds:
\begin{array}[]{c|l|c}j&\text{lower bound for }P_{j}(x)&\text{further lower bound}\\
\hline\cr 0&\frac{5}{4}+(\frac{53}{2}-304x)x-588x^{5}&\frac{6}{5}\\
1&57-316x-250x^{2}&22\\
2&165-1123x-2001x^{3}&50\\
3&56-660x+3186x^{2}-8742x^{3}&13\end{array}
The first row uses 53/2>304(43/500); the last uses
56-660x+3186x^{2}\geq 56-660^{2}/(4\cdot 3186).
The two middle rows follow by setting x=1/10.
Thus every coefficient P_{j} is positive, which proves the lower bound.
∎
